lesson.title: Building Strings from Data: f-strings and Formatting
lesson.summary: F-strings let you embed variables and expressions directly inside a string literal using curly braces, making them Python's clearest way to combine text with data.
lesson.body:
Printing a fixed message is easy, but real programs usually need to weave together literal text and the values of variables, a student's name, a calculated score, today's date, into a single readable string. String formatting is the general name for this task, and Python's modern, preferred tool for it is the f-string, short for "formatted string literal," which builds directly on the string literals you learned in String Basics.

An f-string looks like a normal string literal with the letter f placed immediately before the opening quote, and it allows you to embed expressions directly inside curly braces {} within the text. Trace through this example:

name = "Priya"
score = 87
message = f"{name} scored {score} points."
print(message)

When Python builds this f-string, it does not treat {name} and {score} as literal text. Instead, it evaluates the expression inside each pair of braces, name and score, converts each resulting value to its string form, 'Priya' stays 'Priya' since it is already a string, and 87 becomes the string "87", and splices those converted values into the surrounding literal text. The final result is the string "Priya scored 87 points.", and printing it produces exactly that line. This is dramatically clearer than the older alternative of concatenating pieces with +, which would require name + " scored " + str(score) + " points.", including a manual str() conversion of the number that f-strings handle automatically.

F-strings can hold any valid expression inside the braces, not just a bare variable name, including arithmetic and method calls. f"Doubled: {score * 2}" evaluates score * 2 first, getting 174, then inserts "174" into the text, producing "Doubled: 174". You can even call string methods inline: f"{name.upper()} scored {score} points." evaluates name.upper(), producing "PRIYA", before building the final string, directly reusing the Upper and Lower Methods chapter's tool inside a formatting expression.

F-strings also support format specifications after a colon inside the braces, controlling how a value is displayed. f"{score:.1f}" formats score as a floating-point number with exactly one digit after the decimal point, so if score = 87, this produces "87.0". This is especially useful for money or measurements: f"${19.5:.2f}" produces "$19.50", padding out the decimal places to exactly two even though 19.5 only had one digit to begin with, which matters when displaying currency that should always show cents.

Older code you may encounter uses two earlier formatting styles: the .format() method, "{} scored {}".format(name, score), and the even older % operator, "%s scored %d" % (name, score). Both still work, but f-strings are shorter, easier to read since the variable sits right where it is used rather than in a separate list, and are the style recommended for new code.
